issuer: New York State Workers' Compensation Board
title: Matter of HawthornHealthMulticareCtr
text:
Case # G1053131
Date of Accident: 05/22/2014
District Office: Buffalo
Employer: Hawthorn Health Multicare Ctr
Carrier: Oriska Insurance Co.
Carrier ID No.: W166250
Carrier Case No.: 468-8-1725
Date of Filing of Decision: 05/01/2020
Claimant's Attorney: Jerry A. Gambino
Panel: Clarissa M. Rodriguez
The Full Board, at its meeting on April 21, 2020, considered the above captioned case for Mandatory Full Board Review of the Board Panel Memorandum of Decision filed January 21, 2020.
ISSUE
The issue presented for Mandatory Full Board Review is whether the carrier is liable for prescriptions for Lyrica and Gabapentin.
The Workers' Compensation Law Judge ( WCLJ ) found that the carrier was liable for the cost of Lyrica and Gabapentin.
The Board Panel majority affirmed the WCLJ.
The dissenting Board Panel member would find that the carrier is only liable for any increase in medications caused by claimant's May 22, 2014, work accident.
The carrier filed an application for Mandatory Full Board Review on February 20, 2020, arguing that it should only be liable for any "increases to claimant's previous dosage for Lyrica and Gabapentin from the dosage she was taking prior to the date of injury for an unrelated diagnosis that did not resolve."
The claimant filed a rebuttal on March 9, 2020, arguing that the decision of the Board Panel majority should be affirmed.
Upon review, the Full Board votes to adopt the following findings and conclusions.
FACTS
This claim is established for a May 22, 2014, low back injury. Claimant, the activities director at a nursing home, injured her back while pushing a patient in a wheelchair. Claimant has undergone three spinal surgeries. She underwent a lumbar discectomy with fusion at L4-5 and L5-S1 on April 18, 2016. Claimant underwent anterior discectomy and fusion at L3-4, removal of failed instrumentation at L4-5 and L5-S1, and insertion of anterior fusion at L4 on May 8, 2017. She underwent removal of posterior hardware at L4-5 and L5-S1, laminectomy at L3, reversion laminectomy at L4, and posterior fusion with bone graft at L3-4, L4-5 and L5-S1 on June 26, 2017.
On March 28, 2019, claimant's treating physician, Dr. Gutierrez, filed an MG-2 (Attending Doctor's Request for Approval of Variance and Carrier's Response) seeking a variance from Section F.1.d of the Non-Acute Pain Medical Treatment Guidelines ( NAPMTG ), for the prescription of Lyrica (pregabalin), at a dosage of 200 mg once daily. In support of the variance request, Dr. Gutierrez attached a March 15, 2019, report, in which he indicated that claimant reported that her most recent surgery did not decrease her pain, which she stated was 9 out of 10 at the time of examination. The doctor diagnosed postlaminectomy syndrome and lumbar radiculopathy. Dr. Gutierrez listed among claimant's current medications both Lyrica (300 mg) and Gabapentin (800 mg) and stated that claimant "has been on Lyrica 200mg qd and Celebrex 200mg qd. This is renewed as is because trying to dose as Lyrica 100mg bid-tid was not helpful. [...] With the medications she is able to maintain quality of life and ADL's." Dr. Gutierrez stated that claimant's "[c]urrent medications have proven to improve functional gains in spite of ongoing chronic pain."
The record contains numerous medical records for treatment claimant received prior to her May 22, 2014, work accident. Among those records is an April 23, 2014, report by claimant's treating rheumatologist, Dr. Saldana, who reported that claimant was being seen for polyarthralgia and low back pain. Dr. Saldana stated that claimant was taking 600 mg of Gabapentin three times daily, with some relief of her pain, and that "she still takes Lyrica." The doctor also noted that claimant was also taking 5mg of Oxycodone three times per day, as needed. Dr. Saldana recommended that claimant continue on her current dose of Gabapentin, but made no mention of claimant continuing to take Lyrica, or what dosage of Lyrica that claimant had previously taken. In his previous report, dated January 22, 2014, Dr. Saldana made no mention of claimant taking Lyrica.
Dr. Cash performed a review of claimant's medical records on behalf of the carrier and issued a report dated April 15, 2019. Among the records reviewed by Dr. Cash were reports for treatment claimant received prior to her May 22, 2014, work accident. According to Dr. Cash, claimant was taking Lyrica prior to May 22, 2014, for fibromyalgia. Dr. Cash stated that claimant "prefers once-daily dosing" of Lyrica, "rather than the usual and indicated twice daily dosing. This medication is a good choice for treatment of fibromyalgia and is not causally related to the May 22, 2014, injury as the condition was pre-existing in nature."
On April 25, 2019, the carrier filed a denial of Dr. Gutierrez's request for a variance for Lyrica based on Dr. Cash's April 15, 2019, report. The carrier filed an RFA-2 (Request for Further Action by Carrier/Employer) on May 7, 2019, requesting, among other things, "a hearing regarding the causal relationship" of Lyrica.
By a decision filed June 6, 2019, the WCLJ directed the parties to complete medical depositions and submit the deposition transcripts by August 15, 2019.
Dr. Gutierrez was deposed on July 30, 2019, and testified that she prescribed Lyrica for claimant's lumbar pain. On cross-examination, when asked, "So any medication [claimant] was taking on 4/23/2014 should not be related to this accident, correct?[,]" Dr. Gutierrez responded, Correct" (Deposition Transcript, 7/30/19, p. 13). When asked whether, if claimant had been taking Gabapentin prior to her May 22, 2014, accident, "it would stand to reason that she would still need to take it, even if this accident hadn't occurred, correct?[,]" Dr. Gutierrez responded, "Correct" (p. 15). When asked how Lyrica was causally related to claimant's work-related accident, as she was taking Lyrica prior the accident, Dr. Gutierrez responded that Lyrica is also used for lumbar pain. If claimant was taking Lyrica for lumbar pain prior to her May 22, 2014, work accident, an increased dose may have been needed for exacerbation of her condition. Dr. Gutierrez's medical practice began treating claimant in July of 2018.
At a hearing on August 15, 2019, claimant testified that she was not currently taking Lyrica. Claimant stated that she would rather take Lyrica than hydrocodone, and that if Lyrica were authorized, she could discontinue taking Lortab (acetaminophen and hydrocodone). In a decision filed August 20, 2019, the WCLJ directed claimant to "wean off lortabs and all opiate medications and instead use Lyrica, Gabapentin and Zanaflex for episodic flare ups only." The WCLJ found "the medication causally related to the work accident."
The carrier requested administrative review of the WCLJ's August 20, 2019, decision, arguing that "Lyrica, Gabapentin, and opioid narcotics are not casually related to the injury of record" because claimant used these medications "on a chronic basis" prior to her May 22, 2014, work accident, and presumably would have continued taking those medications even if that accident had never occurred.
In rebuttal, claimant argued that claimant's current medications are causally related to her May 22, 2014, accident, which resulted in three spinal surgeries.
LEGAL ANALYSIS
Workers' Compensation Law ( WCL ) ยง 13(a) requires an employer to pay the cost of medical care and treatment, including medicine, "for such period as the nature of the injury or the process of recovery may require."
The NAPMTG approves the issue of both Lyrica (pregabalin) and Gabapentin for the treatment of neuropathic pain (Section F.1). Claimant's treating physician, Dr. Gutierrez, believed these medications were appropriate to treat claimant's lumbar pain. The carrier does not contend that these medications are not authorized under the NAPMTG and does not argue that those medications are inappropriate to treat claimant's established injury.
The carrier's sole argument is that the Board should find that it is not liable for the cost of prescription medication which would otherwise be appropriate to treat claimant's causally related disability, because claimant had been prescribed that same medication for another condition prior to her work-related injury. Such a finding would be contrary to the "fundamental principle that the Workers' Compensation Law is to be liberally construed to accomplish the economic and humanitarian objects of the act" ( Matter of Smith v Tompkins County Courthouse , 60 NY2d 939 [1983] [internal citations omitted]). As it is not contested that both Lyrica (pregabalin) and Gabapentin are medically necessary and appropriate for the treatment of claimant's work-related low back injury, the carrier is liable for the cost of those medications pursuant to WCL ยง 13(a). That it is possible that claimant might have continued to require the same medication had she not suffered her work injury does not alter this result.
Therefore, the Full Board finds that the preponderance of the evidence in the record supports a finding that the carrier is liable for the cost of prescription Lyrica and Gabapentin, as recommended by Dr. Gutierrez in her March 15, 2019, report. However, subsequent prescriptions of those medications will be subject to the New York Workers' Compensation Formulary , including the prior authorization provisions of the formulary.
CONCLUSION
ACCORDINGLY, the WCLJ decision filed August 20, 2019, is AFFIRMED. No further action is planned by the Board at this time.
